facts.claim: The book opens with John F. Kennedy: between going to bed on October 15, 1962 and waking the next morning, the CIA identified Soviet ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba, ninety miles from US shores (the 'Thirteen Days').
Kennedy's first eighteen months had gone badly: the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961 (the CIA pressured him into it) and being dominated by Khrushchev in Vienna.
His advisors' advice was immediate and emphatic: destroy the missile sites with full military force, followed by a full-scale invasion of Cuba; 'aggression must be met with aggression'.
Kennedy had recently read Barbara Tuchman's The Guns of August, about leaders rushing into World War I and being unable to stop; he wanted everyone to slow down and think.

His handwritten notes during the crisis repeat words: 'Missile. Missile. Missile.', 'Veto. Veto. Veto. Veto.', 'Consensus' six times; on a yellow legal pad he drew two sailboats; on White House stationery he wrote 'We are demanding withdrawal of the missiles.'

He asked advisors why the Russians did this and what advantage they sought. He chose a blockade (nearly half his advisors opposed it) because it preserved options, used 'time as a tool', and called it a 'quarantine'.
facts.source: archive.org full text; Art of Manliness interview

facts.claim: In tense moments he went to the Rose Garden, took long swims and sat in his rocking chair; he left the room so advisors could debate freely.

On October 26, eleven days into the crisis, Khrushchev wrote that the two of them were pulling on a rope with a knot of war in the middle; the Soviets then signalled they would remove the missiles. Kennedy pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove US missiles in Turkey months later.
Napoleon, as a general, had his secretary wait three weeks before opening any correspondence; he loved to note how many 'important' issues had resolved themselves and needed no reply.
facts.source: archive.org full text; Goodreads highlight; Art of Manliness

facts.claim: Holiday notes Napoleon was never negligent of his duties. He told messengers never to wake him with good news; bad news (an unfolding crisis) was to be brought immediately: 'Rouse me instantly, for then there is not a moment to be lost.'
facts.source: archive.org full text; Emerson via tim.blog

facts.claim: Holiday's advice in that chapter (Limit Your Inputs): give things a little space, don't consume news in real time, don't let your inbox lord over your life; the important stays important, the unimportant shows its insignificance. Eisenhower later refused unopened mail and sorted urgent vs important.
The anecdote's origin is Emerson's essay on Napoleon (Representative Men).
facts.source: tim.blog quoting Emerson; Art of Manliness

facts.claim: Holiday quotes Epictetus ('be content to appear clueless or stupid in extraneous matters') and Dorothy Day's 1942 diary ('Turn off your radio, put away your daily paper'); Eisenhower found much was urgent but not important ('Eisenhower Box').

Holiday: lawyers bury the other side in paper, intelligence operatives flood the enemy with propaganda ('analysis paralysis'); advice: don't consume news in real time, be a season or two behind on trends, don't let your inbox lord over your life.
